question: What is a bandit problem, how is a learner's performance measured (regret), and where do bandit models apply?
contributions: Defines the bandit game, policy, environment, environment class and competitor class
Gives an informal definition of regret and the Bernoulli-bandit regret formula
Surveys applications: A/B testing, adverts, recommendation, routing, pricing, waiting problems, resource allocation, tree search

results.claim: Regret for Bernoulli bandits: R_n = n max_a mu_a - E[sum_{t=1}^n X_t], the optimal fixed arm's total mean reward minus the learner's expected reward.

results.claim: A good learner has sublinear regret, R_n = o(n), i.e. lim R_n/n = 0.

limits: Informal definition of regret only (the chapter says so); formal treatment is later.
No sub-Gaussian assumption, concrete upper bound or algorithm appears in this chapter; the sqrt(n) lower/upper rates are stated as forthcoming.
Bandits assume today's choices do not affect tomorrow's options; long-term planning is reinforcement learning (final chapter).
Assumes reward observed every round; otherwise partial monitoring (Ch. 37). Strategic agents are game theory, out of scope.
Authors note they cannot point to an actual clinical-trial use of bandits.
practices: Frame sequential choice under uncertainty as a bandit: learner picks action A_t from history H_{t-1}, then sees reward X_t (p.10).
Measure a learner by regret against a competitor class, aiming for sublinear regret (p.10-11).
Choose environment and competitor classes so regret guarantees are meaningful and low-regret policies exist (p.11).
For adversarial rewards, restrict the competitor class to constant policies rather than constrain the environment (p.12).
Use context (side information) when actions differ per user, e.g. advert placement (p.14).
Real objectives are rarely just clicks; consider satisfaction, diversity, freshness, fairness (p.14).
When only the best arm matters, not accumulated reward, the objective differs from cumulative reward (p.13).

terms.definition: The game is played over n rounds, where n is a positive natural number called the horizon.
A policy is a mapping from histories to actions.
An environment is a mapping from history sequences ending in actions to rewards.
The set E in which the true environment is known to lie.

The regret of the learner relative to a policy pi is the difference between the total expected reward using policy pi for n rounds and the total expected reward collected by the learner over n rounds. The regret relative to a set of policies Pi is the maximum regret relative to any policy in the set.
The set Pi of policies the learner is compared to.
Reward X_t in {0,1} with P(X_t=1 | A_t=a) = mu_a for a vector mu in [0,1]^k.
The maximum regret over all possible environments.
Rewards for each action come from an action-specific distribution independent of previous actions and rewards.
Rewards chosen without knowledge of the learner's actions and lying in a bounded set, with no other assumption.
Action set A subset of R^d, X_t = <a, theta> + eta_t with theta in R^d and eta_t standard Gaussian.
The setting where the reward is not observed in every round.
